result: The left area PF within the left parietal lobe is central for technical reasoning across multiple physical problem-solving tasks. This was demonstrated through whole-brain fMRI analyses showing consistent activation of left area PF in the mechanical problem-solving task, psychotechnical task, and both conditions of the mentalizing task (PHYS-Only and INT+PHYS), confirmed by ROI analyses (all p < 0.001). A conjunction analysis across all four experimental conditions revealed activation only in the left supramarginal gyrus including left area PF.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this as a key finding, with the editor noting 'solid evidence was shown regarding the commonalities and differences across different types of reasoning tasks.' One reviewer stated the study 'offers valuable insights into the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying technical reasoning' and acknowledged that 'additional analyses have enhanced the reliability of the findings.' The consistent activation pattern across tasks was accepted as demonstrating the central role of left area PF.

result: The technical-reasoning network is not recruited during fluid cognition tasks, demonstrating specificity of technical reasoning to the physical domain. The fluid-cognition task activated dorsal prefrontal cortices and medial superior frontal cortices but showed no activation of inferior parietal lobes. ROI analysis confirmed no greater activation of left area PF in the fluid-cognition task (p = 0.35), distinguishing technical reasoning from other forms of non-verbal causal reasoning.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as demonstrating specificity. One reviewer noted the study 'demonstrate[s] the specificity of technical reasoning, finding that area PF is not involved in the fluid-cognition task.' The editor confirmed 'solid evidence was shown regarding the commonalities and differences across different types of reasoning tasks.' This negative result was validated through ROI analysis as requested by reviewers.

result: Technical reasoning and mentalizing networks can interact to solve problems combining social and physical constraints. The INT+PHYS condition activated both left area PF (technical reasoning) and bilateral mentalizing areas (temporoparietal junctions, medial prefrontal cortices, temporal pole). The contrast INT+PHYS > PHYS-Only isolated the mentalizing network without technical-reasoning areas, showing distinct but interacting networks for different domains of causal reasoning.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without challenge. One reviewer acknowledged the study shows 'area PF is central to technical reasoning and plays an essential role in tool-use and non-tool-use physical problem-solving, as well as both conditions of mentalizing tasks.' The demonstration of network interaction was treated as a valid contribution showing how distinct reasoning systems can work together.

result: Correlation analysis revealed significant correlations between all technical reasoning tasks (psychotechnical, PHYS-Only, INT+PHYS; all p < 0.05) but no correlation with the fluid-cognition task (all p > 0.15). This pattern invalidates the 'same-region-but-different-function' interpretation by showing coherent activation patterns across technical reasoning situations.
evaluation: One reviewer raised concerns that correlation analysis 'does not rule out the so-called same region different function interpretation because it relies on correlation—one cannot reverse infer that the left SMG is carrying out the same function across different tasks because the response in that area is more strongly correlated between certain tasks.' The reviewer noted this 'points to that possibility and makes interesting predictions for future studies' but cannot definitively establish common function. Another reviewer noted limitations due to different subject samples and scanning runs.

result: Spatial analysis of activation peaks showed that technical reasoning tasks recruited the same posterior region (left area PF) while fluid cognition activated more anterior regions (left area PFt and postcentral cortex). The y coordinates of technical reasoning task peaks were significantly more posterior than fluid cognition peaks (all p < 0.05), with no differences among the four technical reasoning tasks (all p > 0.05), speaking against the adjacency interpretation.
evaluation: One reviewer questioned the analysis approach, asking 'why restrict the analysis to just the Y coordinate?' and suggested 'a rigorous way to test the adjacency hypothesis is to compute Euclidean distance among X, Y, and Z coordinates between any two tasks.' The reviewer stated 'there is no justification to restrict this analysis to the anterior-posterior dimension only,' indicating the evidence is incomplete for fully addressing the adjacency interpretation.

result: Behavioral results showed that experimental conditions were significantly more difficult than control conditions across all tasks (all p < 0.05), with some participants performing at or below chance level in experimental but not control conditions. This difficulty difference was interpreted as validating the experimental manipulation.
evaluation: Multiple reviewers expressed persistent concerns about differential task difficulty. One reviewer noted 'the concern remains that area PF was driven harder by the experimental task in part due to the more challenging nature of that task' and that the authors' response 'seems to sidestep the central point.' Another reviewer identified 'a major limitation' that 'participants made a button press response only to the last trial in a block,' making it 'not possible for one to know if participants who are at chance are performing differently from participants who are not at chance.' The removal of below-50% performers was deemed 'somewhat helpful' but insufficient.

result: The results demonstrate the existence of a specific cognitive module in the human brain dedicated to materiality, which might be the supporting pillar allowing the accumulation of technical knowledge over generations. This conclusion is drawn from consistent activation of left area PF across physical reasoning tasks.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the core finding of a dedicated neural system for technical reasoning. The editor described it as a 'valuable study' that 'will make a useful contribution to our understanding of some of the computations performed by area PF.' One reviewer stated the work 'enhances our understanding of the neurocognitive basis of technical reasoning that supports advanced technologies.' The speculative aspect about cultural transmission was not challenged.

result: The technical-reasoning network includes left area PF as central, along with additional brain areas such as left IFG and LOTC. The left IFG may integrate multiple constraints from physical situations, while LOTC activation might reflect semantic processes, though these interpretations remain speculative.
evaluation: One reviewer raised a fundamental concern about the interpretation: 'The discussion of the left SMG in the manuscript is prominent and narrowly construed—the left SMG is discussed as if it were 'the' region.' The reviewer noted that 'if one were to relax the threshold...there will be overlapping voxels outside the SMG' and asked 'is there a counterfactual or alternative brain area/network/system not in the left SMG?' This suggests the network characterization may be incomplete or overly focused on one region.

result: The specific activation of left area PF in technical reasoning tasks cannot simply reflect greater difficulty, as ruled out by the fluid-cognition task results which showed no PF activation despite being more difficult than its control condition.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly challenged this interpretation, stating 'this response seems to sidestep the central point of the reviewers' concerns: the fundamental computations that underlie the technical reasoning tasks may also be present in the respective (non technical-reasoning-based) control tasks and drive area PF activations to greater or lesser degrees based on how much they tax those computations.' The reviewer noted that the fluid cognition comparison 'does not mitigate this concern, it just suggests that neither of those tasks tap the same fundamental computations.'
